meta.title: Two contractor workers drowned at an overflowing return-water dam
meta.location: North return-water dam and pump installation
meta.client: Training case study (anonymised; based on a real event)
meta.description: After heavy rain higher up in the catchment, the mine's north return-water dam rose quickly and began to overflow. The mine became aware of the rising level too late, and the pump installation at the dam was being flooded. The engineering manager asked the owner of a small contracting company working on site to help save the pumps. The contractor and two of his workers, none of whom had done work on water before, took an old boat that had been stored on site unused for many years to reach the flooded equipment, with one person on the bank holding a line. The current and wind pushed the boat away faster than the shore attendant could hold it, and it drifted towards the high overflow. Afraid of being carried over the wall, the two workers left the boat to reach the bank. Neither could swim; they underestimated the distance to the dam side and their work clothes and boots hampered them. Both drowned. There was no pre-task risk assessment or job plan, no life jackets or rescue equipment at the dam, and the workers had no training for work on or near water, water rescue or first aid for drowning.

evidence.narrative:
On the afternoon of 14 February, after heavy rain higher up in the catchment, the north return-water dam rose fast and started to overflow. As far as I can tell the control room only noticed when the pump installation was already being flooded; I assume there was no warning from upstream. The engineering manager phoned the owner of the civils contractor who was on site for other work and asked him to help get the pumps out. I believe this was a one-off request in the emergency, but contractors here are often asked to do odd jobs outside their scope because the contractor process is slow.

The contractor and two of his workers used an old aluminium boat that had been lying behind the pump station for years. Nobody I spoke to knows when it was last used or checked. One worker stayed on the bank holding a rope tied to the boat. The shore attendant says the current and the wind pushed the boat towards the spillway and the rope was pulled out of his hands. The two in the boat probably panicked when they saw they were heading for the overflow wall, and they went into the water to swim to the bank. Neither could swim. I think they misjudged the distance to the bank, which looks like 15 to 20 m, and their overalls and safety boots would have dragged them down. There were no life jackets, ring buoys or throw lines at the dam. Nobody did a risk assessment or planned the job, and as far as we know none of them had any training for working on water, rescue or first aid for drowning.

What we do not have yet: drawings of the dam with depths and levels, the spillway height, the positions of the boat and the people, the time line of the alarm and the phone calls, and the wind direction and speed at the time.
evidence.notes: The scene changes fast once the dam level drops: survey the water line, the debris line and the boat position first. Secure the control room level records, phone records and any CCTV today. Interview the shore attendant, the contractor owner and the engineering manager separately and as soon as possible, and record the time line before anything else.

items.item: Surveyed plan and cross-section of the dam: depths, water levels, spillway crest height, pump station position and the bank where the line was held
items.purpose: There are no drawings or measurements yet; needed for distances and the drift path

items.item: Flood debris line and high-water marks around the dam, spillway and pump station
items.purpose: Fixes the peak level; disappears as the water drops

items.item: Position where the boat was found, where the line was held, and where each worker was recovered, with distances
items.purpose: Reconstructs the drift path and the swim distance (assumed 15 to 20 m)

items.item: Wind direction and speed, and flow at the spillway at the time
items.source: Site weather station; national weather service; pump records
items.purpose: Tests the account that current and wind pushed the boat

items.item: Interview the shore attendant (separately, as soon as fit)
items.purpose: Only eyewitness to the drift and to the workers leaving the boat

items.item: Interview the contractor owner
items.purpose: What was asked, what he agreed to, how the boat was chosen, briefing given

items.item: Interview the engineering manager
items.purpose: Why the request was made, what alternatives were considered, who else knew

items.item: Interview the control room operator(s) on shift
items.purpose: When the rising level and the flooding were first noticed and reported

items.item: Interview the recovery and emergency team and the first responders
items.purpose: Response times, rescue equipment available, first aid given

items.item: Post-mortem results and medical reports
items.purpose: Confirms cause of death; any other factors

items.item: The boat: quarantine it; record condition, leaks, oars or motor, capacity plate, rope attachment point
items.purpose: Was the boat fit for use? Was it ever inspected?

items.item: The rope or line used from the bank: length, type, condition, how it was held or tied
items.purpose: Tests whether the shore control could ever have held the boat

items.item: Clothing, boots and PPE worn by the two workers
items.purpose: Tests the account that PPE hampered swimming

items.item: Any life jackets, ring buoys or throw lines anywhere on site, and where they are kept
items.purpose: Was life-saving equipment available at all?

items.item: Dam operating manual or procedure, including flood trigger levels and the emergency plan for the dam
items.purpose: Was a flood response defined?

items.item: Contract, scope of work, site appointment and induction records of the contractor and the two workers
items.purpose: Tests scope creep: was this work within the contract?

items.item: Records of other jobs asked of contractors outside their scope in the last 12 months
items.source: Contractor management office; purchase orders; job cards
items.purpose: Tests the belief that scope creep is routine

items.item: Contractor management procedure and how long onboarding and approval normally take
items.purpose: Tests "the contractor process is slow"

items.item: Any risk assessment, permit or job plan for the task, and the site rule for work on or near water
items.purpose: Confirms that no pre-task risk assessment was done

items.item: Training records of the contractor and workers: water safety, rescue, first aid, swimming ability
items.purpose: Tests the account that nobody was trained

items.item: Asset or stores records for the old boat: when it came to site, last use, any inspection
items.purpose: Why was an unused boat available for use?

items.item: Previous incidents, near misses or audit findings for the dam, the pump station or work on water
items.purpose: Was the risk known before?

items.item: Dam level, pump and alarm logs (SCADA/telemetry) for the day
items.purpose: Time line: when the level rose and when the alarm (if any) went off

items.item: Phone and radio records of the calls between the control room, engineering manager and contractor owner
items.purpose: Time line of the request and the response

items.item: Rainfall data for the upper catchment for the 24 hours before (weather service, upstream gauges)
items.purpose: Tests the assumption that no upstream warning was available

items.item: CCTV covering the dam, pump station or access road
items.purpose: Independent record of the boat drift and the time line

items.item: Photos or videos taken by anyone on site during the event, on phones
items.purpose: May show positions, conditions and wind
